SquareCells, developed and published by Matthew Brown, is a clever and engaging puzzle game that challenges players with a fresh take on logic-based grid puzzles. Building upon the foundations of his previous hit, Hexcells, this title presents a new geometric twist by using square grids instead of hexagonal ones, which adds a different kind of complexity and strategy. The game strikes a satisfying balance between simplicity and depth, making it accessible to newcomers while offering enough challenge to keep seasoned puzzle enthusiasts hooked for hours.

At its core, SquareCells tasks players with uncovering hidden patterns on a grid using numerical clues that provide information about how many cells in each row, column, or specific area should be filled or marked. The gameplay loop is elegantly simple: deduce which squares are “filled” or “empty” based on the numerical hints, gradually revealing the correct pattern. What sets SquareCells apart is the way it combines elements from classic puzzles like Sudoku and Nonograms but adds its unique mechanics, such as the introduction of “empty cells” that must be deliberately marked and various clue types that require a nuanced understanding of logic to interpret correctly.

The progression throughout SquareCells is well-paced, with puzzles that start out relatively straightforward to help players familiarize themselves with the game’s rules and gradually ramp up in difficulty. Each puzzle is designed with meticulous attention to detail, requiring increasingly complex logical deductions and careful consideration of multiple overlapping clues. This layered complexity ensures that the game never feels repetitive or frustrating but instead encourages critical thinking and pattern recognition skills. The satisfaction derived from solving particularly challenging puzzles is immense, making it a rewarding experience for those who appreciate cerebral gameplay.

Visually, SquareCells adopts a clean, minimalist design that enhances clarity and focus. The grids are presented with crisp lines and subtle color coding, which helps players easily distinguish between different types of cells and clues without unnecessary distraction. The user interface is intuitive and responsive, allowing for smooth interaction whether using a mouse or a touchscreen. This minimalist aesthetic not only reinforces the game’s cerebral nature but also creates a calming atmosphere that contrasts nicely with the mental effort required to crack each puzzle.

Complementing the gameplay and visuals is a soothing soundtrack that helps maintain concentration and reduces the stress that can sometimes accompany challenging puzzles. The ambient music is unobtrusive but pleasant, creating a meditative environment conducive to extended play sessions. Sound effects are minimal but effective, providing subtle feedback for player actions such as marking or clearing cells.

SquareCells also offers excellent replay value. With over a hundred puzzles spread across multiple levels, it provides many hours of challenging and thoughtful gameplay. For players who enjoy mastering logic puzzles or are fans of brain teasers, this title is a compelling addition to their collection. The game encourages exploration of different solving strategies, making each playthrough unique as players refine their approaches and discover new methods of deduction.

In summary, SquareCells is a thoughtfully designed puzzle game that successfully combines elegance, challenge, and accessibility. Matthew Brown’s ability to craft compelling logic puzzles with clean design and an inviting atmosphere shines through in this title. Whether you are a fan of logic puzzles or simply looking for a mentally stimulating way to pass the time, SquareCells offers a deeply satisfying experience that rewards patience, observation, and logical thinking.

My opinion of SquareCells is very similar to a comment I have about HexCells: what if Picross withheld certain details that were vital to completing the puzzle? This game attempts to make up for removing clues about certain columns and rows by adding numbers inside of certain cells that indicate contiguous segments. Despite this, every puzzle after the first few left me thinking that I simply didn’t have enough information to figure out the solution, resulting in a frustrating loop of trial and error. Also, where Picross-type games often let you mark squares with placeholders in order to experiment without cost, SquareCells forces you to mark each square as “keep” or “remove”, with an immediate penalty if you pick the wrong one. On the plus side, I was able to complete this one faster than most of Matthew Brown’s other games.

Coming from the minesweeper-like Hexcells trilogy I was curious about what other kinds of logic based games Matthew had in store. Since the bundle included 2 more games this one was next and upon booting it up I noticed the direction was different this time even if the presentation didn't appear to be that way. Let’s see how it went down.

Unlike the previous games, this one is based on nonograms, also known as Picross. These are the classic grid based logic puzzles where you need to color certain cells based on certain indications, usually following numbers. In that sense you could make the correlation to minesweeper and if you’ve played the previous games some of those variations are related as well. In fact, they are there to make the game more challenging although not so much to alienate the casual gamer.

Regarding its presentation, after adjusting the display resolution properly to your corresponding graphical set up which may not be as easy as it sounds, the minimalist and clean Helvetica facade brushes away any type of distraction, constituting the perfect environment for this kind of puzzler. As a result you can play this on a coffee break, with some tea and toast on the side, even while listening to a podcast with people whose opinions you may not agree with. It's all fair game in order to get those lovely 3 stars at the end and the chime of level completion.

In short, if you want to try a tiny albeit engaging logic variation to nonograms or you’re in need to perfect games to increase your Steam profile statistics, here's an offer.

SquareCells provides the Hexcells treatment to picross (minus the picture element), i.e. adding additional complexity to the puzzles. Compared to actual picross games, the SquareCells grid never gets particularly large, never getting any larger than 14x14.

Like the Hexcells trilogy, SquareCells contains 36 puzzles, some of which have one or two very hard-to-figure-out moves you need to make that need very close attention to work out. The Hexcells Infinite random generation hasn't been carried forward to this one, however, so replayability is limited by that.

Unfortunately, whilst the puzzles themselves are fun and tricky, and like Hexcells, are possible without guesswork, the game is let down a little by it's presentation, primarily in graphic for flagged cells not being distinct enough to make out easily, particularly under certain colour schemes. Plus, some of the wording of the tutorials could be better, particularly when explaining the numbers within the cells themselves, as it took me a bit to actually figure out that particular mechanic. For this reason, and for the limited short-term replayability, I'm only giving this one a 7/10. Good, but some flaws.
